concept.name: Wyckoff method
concept.definition: A discretionary technical-analysis framework developed by Richard D. Wyckoff in the early twentieth century that interprets price action, volume, and time to judge the supply/demand balance and hypothesized campaigns of large institutional operators. It organizes market movement into accumulation, markup, distribution, and markdown phases and is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Big players move markets by quietly building and unwinding large positions; if you can read their footprints in price and volume, you can trade in their direction instead of being trapped by them.
concept.mechanics: Practitioners apply a five-step approach: assess the broad market trend and its position, select stocks stronger (or weaker) than the market, require a sufficient cause measured by point-and-figure counts, confirm readiness with Wyckoff's nine buying or selling tests, and time entry with turns in the market index. Within trading ranges, events (PS, SC, AR, ST, springs, SOS/LPS) and phases (A-E) are labeled to infer whether accumulation or distribution is occurring.
concept.failure_modes: Phase and event labeling is subjective and often clear only in hindsight; ranges can extend, morph, or resolve opposite to the labeled interpretation, and the framework assumes the presence of dominant institutional campaigns that may not apply in thinly traded or highly fragmented markets.
concept.misconceptions: It is not a mechanical signal system with fixed rules, and its 'laws' are heuristics rather than physical laws; Wyckoff himself cautioned that the market never behaves exactly the same way twice.
concept.example: An analyst labels a six-month sideways range after a long decline as accumulation (selling climax, secondary tests, a low-volume spring, then a sign of strength), takes a long position on the last point of support, and projects a price target from a point-and-figure count of the range.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett; schematics edited by Henry O. Pruden)
